subject: physics

moments.title: Maxwell predicts electromagnetic waves
moments.body:
Maxwell's equations predict that any oscillating electric current must produce electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light. The prediction sits as theoretical speculation for 23 years.

Maxwell dies in 1879. The waves are still hypothetical.
moments.takeaway: A bold theoretical prediction sits unconfirmed for over two decades.

moments.title: Hertz sets up the apparatus
moments.body:
Hertz, then 30, builds a transmitter: a Ruhmkorff induction coil driving an oscillating spark between two brass spheres separated by a small gap. The spark creates rapidly oscillating currents — and so, by Maxwell, electromagnetic waves.

His receiver is a simple wire loop with a small spark gap. When waves from the transmitter reach the loop, a tiny spark jumps the receiver gap. Hertz can darken the room to see it more easily.
moments.takeaway: An elegant apparatus reduces the question to one observable: do tiny sparks appear at the receiver?

moments.title: Hertz detects, measures, characterises
moments.body:
Hertz systematically maps the waves: he measures their wavelength (around 4 metres for his apparatus), shows they reflect off metal sheets, refract through pitch prisms, polarise through grids of parallel wires, and produce standing-wave patterns by interference. All the optical properties Maxwell's theory predicts.

He publishes 14 papers in 1888. Maxwell's prediction is fully confirmed.

quote.text: It's of no use whatsoever... we just have these mysterious electromagnetic waves that we cannot see with the naked eye. But they are there.
quote.attrib: Heinrich Hertz, on being asked the practical value of his work

moments.takeaway: Electromagnetic waves are real. They behave optically. They can be generated and detected in the lab.

moments.title: Marconi commercialises radio
moments.body:
Within seven years of Hertz's death (1894), Marconi has built up the basic technology to commercial scale: long-distance wireless telegraphy. By 1901 he transmits the letter 'S' across the Atlantic, from Cornwall to Newfoundland.

Marconi wins the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics. Hertz (who died young of an infection at 36) is honoured posthumously: the unit of frequency, the hertz, is named for him in 1930.
moments.takeaway: Pure physics becomes a global communication infrastructure within a generation.

now.title: The electromagnetic spectrum today
now.body:
The electromagnetic spectrum — radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays — is all one phenomenon, differing only in wavelength. The full spectrum spans more than 20 orders of magnitude. Mobile phones use ~1 GHz; FM radio ~100 MHz; Wi-Fi ~2.4 GHz or ~5 GHz; 5G up to ~30 GHz; medical X-rays ~10 to the 18 Hz.

Global telecommunications, broadcasting, navigation (GPS), remote sensing (weather radar, satellite imagery), heating (microwave ovens), and astronomy (radio telescopes through gamma-ray observatories) all use parts of the spectrum.
now.open_questions: Can higher-frequency parts of the spectrum (terahertz, mm-wave) be exploited for next-generation wireless networks? Can quantum-mechanical control of single radio-frequency photons (quantum radio) become useful?

reflection: Hertz was confident his discovery had no practical applications. Within a generation, radio reshaped global communication. How often do scientists drastically misjudge the future impact of their work — and what does this tell us about funding 'curiosity-driven' research?
